BONE SARCOMA. The commonest primary malignant tumour of bone is osteosarcoma (osteogenic sarcoma) which accounts for about 3 to 4% of all childhood ma- lignancies. It is composed of malignant osteoblasts which form an osteoid matrix within which new bone formation may occur. Most osteosarcomas are aggres- sive high-grade malignancies which destroy overlying cortical bone and invade adjacent soft tissue, as well as spreading along the medulla. Metastasis, almost exclu- sively via the vascular system to the lungs and other dis- tant sites, is usual and occurs early. The main therapy is surgery, with an increasing trend to more conservative, limb-sparing operations rather than amputation. Adjuvant chemotherapy is an important com- ponent of therapy, however, as metastasis of the tumour is common.1-4 Combinations of cisplatin, doxorubicin, ifos- famide, and high-dose methotrexate are recommended.3,4 Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is often given before surgery to attack micrometastases, shrink the primary tumour and enable evaluation of the tumour response.3,5 Aggressive treatment regimens can result in long-term relapse-free survival rates of 70%, although patients with overt meta- static disease at presentation have a poorer prognosis.4,5 Osteosarcomas are relatively resistant to radiation thera- py;4 however, for unresectable high-grade osteosarcoma, radiotherapy followed by adjuvant chemotherapy is rec- ommended.3 Like osteosarcoma, Ewing’s sarcoma is seen mainly in adolescents and older children. It is a round cell tumour that most often arises in the pelvis or the long bones of the limbs. There may be diffuse erosion of the bone and marked periosteal reaction. It spreads through the medul- lary cavity, and metastases to lung and other bones are common. Initial treatment is neoadjuvant chemotherapy for several months.3,4 Combinations of cyclophosphamide, ifosfa- mide, etoposide, doxorubicin, and vincristine are recom- mended,3,4 given good results from addition of ifosfamide and etoposide to standard regimens.4,6 Dactinomycin has also been used in standard regimens,4,6 although its use for localised disease is controversial.4 Typically, patients are then given local therapy (surgery, radiation, or both), with additional adjuvant chemotherapy.3,4 Ewing’s sarcoma is relatively radiosensitive,4 and unresponsive or progressive
